title: On-call & Incident Response Playbook — Runbooks, Rotations, and Comms Templates
author: Avery Brooks
content:
Purpose
This playbook provides a single-source reference for Redwood Inference on-call operations and incident response. It contains the incident lifecycle, runbook templates, on-call rotation guidance, postmortem expectations, game day practices, and customer/status-page communication templates. The goal is to reduce time-to-detection, standardize escalation paths, and ensure consistent, transparent communications to internal stakeholders and customers.

Scope
- Applies to all production-facing services and critical internal platforms (billing, auth, control plane, model-serving).
- Includes hosted API, Dedicated control plane, and Private deployment coordination where Redwood is the support contact.
- Non-production incidents (dev/staging) should follow a lighter-weight process documented in the eng-platform team wiki.

Roles and responsibilities
- Primary Oncall: owns alert triage, initial mitigation, and engagement of secondary/engineers on rotation.
- Secondary/Responder: helps investigate, implements mitigations, and owns shards of long-running fixes.
- Incident Commander (IC): assigned for Sev-1/Sev-2 to coordinate cross-team work, comms, and timeline.
- Subject Matter Experts (SMEs): product, infra, security, and networking specialists who might be paged for domain-specific failures.
- Communications Owner: drafts and publishes status page and customer-facing notifications (typically Support or SRE).

Incident severity definitions
1) Sev-1 (Critical): widespread outage or data loss affecting >50% of customers or critical business functions. Requires immediate oncall escalation and IC assignment.
2) Sev-2 (High): degraded/widespread impact affecting a significant subset of customers or critical SLAs; repair required ASAP.
3) Sev-3 (Medium): partial loss of functionality or elevated error rates with limited user impact.
4) Sev-4 (Low): informational or minor issues with no measurable customer impact.

Incident lifecycle (high-level steps)
1. Detect & Alert
   - Alerts arrive via PagerDuty/Slack/Monitoring. Oncall acknowledges within configured SLA (default: 5 minutes for Sev-1, 30 minutes for Sev-2).
2. Triage
   - Determine scope, affected customers, approximate root cause hypothesis, and assign severity.
3. Mitigate
   - Apply quick mitigations (traffic routing, scale-up, rollback, circuit-breakers, fallback models). Document commands executed.
4. Escalate & Engage
   - Page SMEs, assign Incident Commander for Sev-1/Sev-2, and create an incident channel (#incident-<YYYYMMDD>-<service>).
5. Communicate
   - Publish status page update and internal summary within 30 minutes of IC assignment for Sev-1, 60 minutes for Sev-2. Use templates in the "Status & Customer Comms" section.
6. Recovery & Validation
   - Confirm system health via SLIs and synthetic checks, notify stakeholders, and close incident when stable.
7. Postmortem & Follow-ups
   - Create an RCA within 72 hours (draft) and publish a final postmortem with action items and owners within 14 days.

Escalation matrix (summary)
- Primary oncall -> Secondary (10 minutes) -> Team lead (20 minutes) -> IC (if Sev-1/Sev-2) -> CTO/Head of Engineering (if >60 minutes or large customer impact).

On-call rotation & expectations
- Rotation model: 1-week primary rotations with 2-week secondary on-call windows (example schedule: Mon 00:00 UTC — Mon 00:00 UTC).
- Coverage: follow-the-sun model supported by regional responders; nights/weekends are covered by rotation with automatic escalation.
- Handover checklist (every shift):
  1. Review active incidents and assigned follow-ups.
  2. Check pending alerts and long-running runbooks.
  3. Confirm access and escalation contacts are current.
- Time commitment: expected to respond to pages within 5 minutes (Sev-1) and 30 minutes (Sev-2) during shift. Notify your manager for planned unavailability >24 hours and arrange a swap using the oncall rota tool.

Runbook template (every production service should have one)
- Runbook metadata (top of doc): service name, owner, pager, runbook version, last updated.
- Sections:
  1) Quick summary: one-paragraph description of the service and primary failure modes.
  2) Detection: key alerts/metrics, thresholds, and pager rules.
  3) Impact assessment: how to measure customer impact (SLIs, metrics, request paths).
  4) Immediate mitigations: prioritized steps with commands and expected outcomes.
  5) Full recovery steps: more invasive fixes, rollbacks, and migration instructions.
  6) Post-incident checks: verification commands, dashboards to inspect, and smoke tests.
  7) Contacts & escalation: oncall, engineers, team lead, and cross-team contacts.

Example runbook excerpt for "model-serving" (abridged)
- Metadata: service: model-serving; owner: eng-serving-runtime; pager: pagerduty-service-id-abc123; version: v1.4; last_updated: 2026-01-10
- Quick summary: real-time token generation service that serves hosted API and dedicated pools. Common failures: GPU OOMs, kernel regressions, KV cache corruption, networking flaps.
- Detection:
  - 5xx error rate > 2% for 5 minutes -> page
  - Median p99 latency > 800ms for 2 minutes
- Immediate mitigations (ordered):
  1. Route traffic to fallback model: `redwood route --service model-serving --to model-serving-fallback`
  2. Restart affected worker group: `kubectl rollout restart deployment/model-serving-worker -n prod`
  3. Evict suspect pods: `kubectl delete pod <pod-id> -n prod`
  4. If OOMs, reduce batch size via remote flag: `redwood config set model-serving.batch_size 8`
- Post-incident checks:
  - Verify p99 latency < 300ms across regions for 15 minutes
  - Confirm KV cache hit rate > 85% and no increased error logs in the last 30 minutes

Postmortem (RCA) template and expectations
- Title, Sev, date/time window, incident owner (IC), services affected, customer impact summary.
- Timeline: numbered events with UTC timestamps, who did what, and links to logs/PRs/dashboards.
- Root cause hypothesis and evidence supporting it.
- Contributing factors (people, process, tooling, engineering debt).
- Mitigations applied during incident.
- Action items (owner, due date, priority).
- Severity and priority of remediation work (e.g., P0: fix within 7 days; P1: 30 days).
- Postmortem publishing expectations: draft shared with reviewers within 72 hours; final postmortem published to Confluence and linked to customer incident when complete (14-day target).

Game days and training
- Frequency: quarterly cross-team game days run by eng-sre. One public, one private for enterprise integrations per year.
- Goals: validate runbooks, test escalation paths, exercise status page workflows and customer comms, and measure MTTR.
- Anatomy of a game day: scenario design, pre-brief, simulation window, post-game retrospective.
- Game day checklist: notify stakeholders, create simulated incidents in staging, run through comms templates, and record elapsed times for key milestones.

Status page and customer communications templates
- Status page best practices:
  - Update early and often: customers prefer transparency even if root cause is unknown.
  - Use consistent language and severity labels aligned to internal Sev definitions.
  - Include: short summary, affected components, customer impact, mitigation steps in progress, ETA (if known), and last updated time.
- Internal status update cadence for Sev-1/Sev-2: 30-minute cadence until mitigated, then hourly until stable.

Sample status page entry (template)
- Title: Degraded model-serving response times (region: us-west-2)
- Impact: Customers experiencing elevated latencies when calling text-generation endpoints. Estimated 40% of requests impacted; no data loss reported.
- Status: Investigating
- Mitigation in progress: Rolling traffic to fallback model and scaling worker replicas.
- ETA: 30 minutes
- Last updated: 2026-02-10T15:32:00Z

Customer-facing email / support ticket template (short)
- Subject: Incident update — elevated latency for text-generation (us-west-2)
- Body: Hello, we are investigating an incident impacting text-generation latency in us-west-2. We have identified a partial degradation and are routing traffic to fallback models while we stabilize replicas. We will post updates on our status page and follow up with a full postmortem.

Internal incident Slack comms template
- Channel topic: #incident-<YYYYMMDD>-<service>
- Initial message: [Sev-1] Incident created for model-serving — paged at 2026-02-10T15:12Z by PagerDuty. Primary oncall: @alice, Secondary: @bob. IC: @charlie. Brief: elevated p99 latency and 5xx spike in us-west-2.

Runbook and playbook maintenance
- Ownership: every runbook must list a primary owner (engineer) and one backup. Owners are responsible for quarterly review and updates.
- Automated reminders: the runbook tool will send quarterly review reminders; owners must confirm or update content within 14 days.
- Versioning: store runbooks in Confluence with a version header and maintain a changelog line for each update.

Metrics and SLOs to monitor during incidents
| Metric | Threshold | Action |
|---|---:|---|
| p99 latency (text-generation) | 800ms | Page (Sev-1) |
| 5xx rate (api) | 2% | Page (Sev-1) |
| Error budget burn (daily) | 5% | Notify SRE and Product |
| Model-serving KV cache hit rate | 80% | Investigate cache degradation |

Runbook checklist for creating a new service runbook
1. Fill metadata and owner contact.
2. List top 5 failure modes and detection criteria.
3. Add CLI/infra commands for mitigation and recovery.
4. Add post-incident verification steps and dashboards.
5. Conduct a tabletop review with SRE and product.

Post-incident follow-up and tracking
- Action items must be tracked in the team backlog with labels: incident, postmortem, remediation. Owners are expected to estimate and schedule work during the next sprint planning.
- High-priority fixes (P0/P1) require an owner and a target completion date in the postmortem.
- Quarterly reliability review: eng-sre summarizes incident trends, MTTR, and completed remediations for leadership.

Appendix A — Pager and contact quick reference
- PagerDuty: Redwood-prod-pager (link stored in team vault)
- Oncall rotation owner: eng-sre@redwood.com
- SRE lead: Ethan Walker (@ethan)

Appendix B — Useful CLI commands and diagnostics
- Check model-serving pods: `kubectl get pods -n prod -l app=model-serving -o wide`
- Tail logs for a pod: `kubectl logs -f <pod-id> -n prod`
- Rollback deployment: `kubectl rollout undo deployment/model-serving-worker -n prod`
- Route traffic to fallback: `redwood route --service model-serving --to model-serving-fallback`
